description: A composite group that combines a data table (Table IV) with four grey-scale SEM fractographs (Fig. 14 a-d). Table IV lists hardness (BHN) and dynamic fracture toughness, DFT (kJ/m²), for Fe-30Mn-9Al-XSi-0.9C steels at four Si/P levels — 0.59% Si, 0.002% P; 1.07% Si, 0.001% P; 1.56% Si, 0.002% P; 0.94% Si, 0.043% P — plus a reference Cast 4130, under the heat treatments "Solution Treated at 1050°C 2 h", "Aged at 530°C" (10-90 h) and "Quenched and tempered". Solution-treated alloys reach 715 kJ/m² (0.59% Si, 200 ± 10 BHN) and 700 kJ/m² (1.56% Si, 208 ± 10 BHN); aging at 530°C raises hardness to 295-375 BHN while DFT falls to 95-376 kJ/m². The four secondary-electron SEM panels, each with a 50 µm scale bar, are fracture surfaces of Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C: (a) 1.07% Si and (b) 1.56% Si aged to ~300 BHN, (c) 1.07% Si and (d) 1.56% Si aged to ~350 BHN. They show the ductile-to-brittle transition — (a,b) dimpled ductile rupture, (c,d) brittle transgranular cleavage facets bearing {111} slip traces. The group argues that age hardening and higher Si content both lower DFT and promote brittle cleavage.

Rows group four Si/P alloy variants (0.59% Si 0.002% P; 1.07% Si 0.001% P; 1.56% Si 0.002% P; 0.94% Si 0.043% P) and a Cast 4130 reference, under solution-treated (1050°C 2 h), aged at 530°C for various times, and quenched-and-tempered conditions.
SEM fractograph (secondary electron), 50 µm scale bar, of 1.07% Si Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C aged to ~300 BHN, showing fully ductile dimpled rupture with coarse equiaxed dimples and tear ridges.
SEM fractograph, 50 µm scale bar, of 1.56% Si aged to ~300 BHN: a mixed surface combining ductile dimpled regions with flat facets and secondary cracks.
SEM fractograph, 50 µm scale bar, of 1.07% Si aged to ~350 BHN, dominated by brittle transgranular cleavage facets with river patterns and fine parallel slip traces on favorably oriented facets.
SEM fractograph, 50 µm scale bar, of 1.56% Si aged to ~350 BHN, showing large brittle transgranular cleavage facets with prominent {111} slip traces and tear ridges.

observations.observation: The group is composite: one image is a table with the columns Alloy, Heat treatment, Hardness (BHN) and DFT (kJ/m²), and four images are grey-scale SEM fractographs each carrying a white 50 µm scale bar.

Table IV reports for 1.56% Si, 0.002% P a solution-treated (1050°C 2 h) hardness of 208 ± 10 BHN and DFT of 700 kJ/m², and for 0.59% Si, 0.002% P a solution-treated hardness of 200 ± 10 BHN and DFT of 715 kJ/m².
Table IV shows that aging at 530°C for 90 h raises the 0.59% Si, 0.002% P alloy to 366 ± 9 BHN while its DFT drops to 95 ± 15 kJ/m².
Among the age-hardened low-P alloys listed in Table IV the highest DFT is 376 ± 23 kJ/m² (1.07% Si, 0.001% P, aged 530°C 13 h) and the lowest is 95 ± 15 kJ/m² (0.59% Si, aged 530°C 90 h).
Cast 4130 quenched-and-tempered reference values in Table IV are 350 BHN with 94 kJ/m² and 330 BHN with 136 kJ/m².
The 0.94% Si, 0.043% P alloy aged at 530°C 10 h is listed at 340 ± 10 BHN and 100 kJ/m² (no uncertainty given for DFT).
SEM panel (a) shows entirely ductile dimpled rupture, with coarse equiaxed dimples separated by tear ridges and no extensive flat facets.
SEM panel (b) shows a mixed fracture surface combining ductile dimpled regions with flat, cleavage-like facets and secondary cracking.
SEM panels (c) and (d) are dominated by brittle transgranular cleavage facets showing river patterns and fine parallel slip traces on favorably oriented facets.
The caption states that panels (a and c) are 1.07% Si and (b and d) are 1.56% Si, aged at 530°C to a hardness range of 300 BHN (a and b) and 350 BHN (c and d).
The caption states that {111} slip traces are noted on favorably oriented cleavage facets, suggesting fracture by decohesion of glide planes.
The caption states the fracture surfaces show a transition from ductile failure to brittle transgranular cleavage-type fracture with increased age hardening and silicon content.
The citing text states that in the solution-treated condition DFT was statistically equivalent for the low-phosphorus (<0.003% P) 1.07 and 1.56% Si specimens, averaging around 700 kJ/m².
The citing text states that increasing Si from 1.07% to 1.56% decreased the DFT of age-hardened steels and increased the propensity for brittle fracture.

unreadable_items: Panel letters (a)-(d) are not printed on the SEM micrographs; the assignment of each micrograph to a panel label is inferred from fracture texture and the caption, not read from the image.
Table IV caption note reads 'Uncertainty reported for test sample greater than four and represents one sample standard deviation' - the low-resolution phrasing is partially readable.
